title: Audit log: authentication and article post events
description:
Append-only audit log recording who authenticated, what commands they ran, and what articles they posted — separate from the application log, suitable for compliance and forensics.

Why this issue exists:
Enterprise buyers ask 'who posted that?' The application log answers this only if DEBUG is enabled and log rotation has not yet swept the relevant window. A dedicated audit log provides a durable, structured, compliance-grade record without requiring DEBUG-level application logging in production.

Scope:
Audit events (written to a separate append-only log file or table, never to stdout):
- auth_success: timestamp, service, remote_ip, username, auth_method (password|client_cert|bearer_token|oidc)
- auth_failure: timestamp, service, remote_ip, username_attempted, reason
- article_posted: timestamp, service, remote_ip, username, message_id, newsgroups, cid
- article_rejected: timestamp, service, remote_ip, username, reason, message_id (if parsed)
- config_reloaded: timestamp, admin_ip (or 'sighup'), fields_changed
- admin_action: timestamp, admin_ip, endpoint, method

Storage: configurable — file (append-only JSONL, one event per line) or SQLite table in a dedicated audit.db. Never in the main application log stream.

Retention: audit log is never rotated or deleted by the daemon. Retention is the operator's responsibility (ship to S3, CloudWatch Logs, Splunk, etc.).

Acceptance criteria:
- Every successful AUTHINFO USER/PASS produces an auth_success audit event
- Every POST produces an article_posted event with the CID of the stored article
- Audit log file is append-only: the daemon opens it with O_APPEND and never truncates
- Audit events are valid JSONL: one JSON object per line, no multi-line values
- Application log level changes do not affect audit log output — audit events are always written
